about: A workflow every account can find and run: make a short explainer video on any topic, pitched at one learner's level, with a consistent animated character that speaks the lesson, using only free or open-source tools that run on the person's own computer. One workflow-recipe row in the shape of the shared recipe shelf (job, input_schema, ordered steps, each with do, submit and checks).

payload.produces: A finished explainer video for one learner on one topic; the video itself, or a cut of it, is shareable.
payload.label: Make a personalised explainer video on any topic for a learner
payload.job: Turn a topic and a description of one learner (what they know, what they want, how long they will watch) into a finished explainer video: a lesson pitched at that learner, a spoken track, word-exact timing, one consistent animated character whose mouth follows the voice, one picture per spoken line, and a deterministic render. Every part uses a free or open-source tool that runs on the person's own computer, so a video for one more learner costs only the computer's time. Every number the video states comes from the lesson text the person's AI wrote or from a source it names; the AI never invents a statistic.

source.name: A post showing a personalised lesson video made in about 15 minutes for a few cents with paid voice, image, timing and animation services
source.note: The post's cost and time are the author's claim and were not verified. This recipe replaces each paid service with a free tool the person already has: voice from a local speech model or the person's own cloned voice, timing from a local speech-to-text model, the character from a local image model with a reference-image method, mouth movement from the voice's loudness, and the render from an open-source HTML video renderer.

topic.description: What the video teaches, in a few words

level.description: What the learner already knows about the topic, in their own terms

goal.description: What the learner wants to be able to do or understand afterwards

age_or_background.description: Anything that changes the words or examples that will land

language.description: The language of the video; defaults to the language of the topic

length_seconds.description: How long the video should run; defaults to 90

voice.description: stock-voice uses a local speech model's built-in voice; my-own-voice clones the voice of the person running this workflow from their own clean recording

own_voice_reference.description: Path to a clean recording of the person's own voice and the exact words said in it, only when voice is my-own-voice

character_description.description: Who the on-screen character is, in a sentence; the AI invents a simple one if left out

steps.title: Pitch the lesson at this learner
steps.do: Write the lesson plan in the learner's terms. Line 1 names the learner's problem in under 6 words. Line 2 promises the payoff. Then 3 to 7 points, each answering one question the learner would ask next, in order, starting from what the learner already knows (input learner.level) and ending at what they want (input learner.goal). Finish with one closing line that pays off line 1. Choose the number of points so the spoken total fits length_seconds at about 2.5 spoken words per second (90 seconds when length_seconds is left out). For every fact or number, name where it comes from (a page or document you read in this run); if you cannot name one, write the point without the number. Show the plan to the person and wait for a go-ahead before spending computer time on voice or pictures.

source.description: Where a fact or number in this answer comes from; empty when the answer has none

steps.title: Write the spoken lines, one picture each
steps.do: Turn the plan into spoken lines: each line is one short sentence a person would say aloud, and each line gets exactly one picture idea (one line equals one visual). For every number, write two forms side by side: shown (as the caption prints it, for example '11:58 PM') and spoken (as the voice must say it, for example 'eleven fifty-eight P M'). Write the picture idea as what the character is doing or what is on screen, never as camera jargon. Keep the total of spoken words within the length the plan allows.

checks.says: No spoken line is a placeholder

steps.title: Record the voice with a free local speech model
steps.do: Pick the voice. If input voice is 'stock-voice' (or left out), use a local speech model from the person's tools, for example Kokoro-82M (weights licensed Apache-2.0, read from the model card) run on the person's computer. If input voice is 'my-own-voice', use a local voice-cloning model such as Chatterbox (repository MIT-licensed, read from its licence file) with input own_voice_reference as the reference and the exact words said in it; this clones only the voice of the person running the workflow from their own recording, never anyone else's. Read line L1 aloud in three candidate voices (or three settings of the one cloned voice), pick the clearest for this learner, then speak every line's 'spoken' text, one audio file per line. When cloning, speak phrase by phrase so a long line cannot drift, and compare each result to the reference voice with a speaker-embedding check before keeping it. Cap any silence longer than 0.24 seconds to 0.24 seconds, but only where a loudness check in 0.03-second windows confirms it is silent. Save each line as an audio file and record its path and length.

tool.description: The local model that spoke, with the licence read from its model card or repository

checks.says: Every written line has its own audio file

steps.title: Time every word with a free local speech-to-text model
steps.do: Transcribe each audio file with word timestamps using a local speech-to-text model from the person's tools, for example faster-whisper (MIT-licensed, read from its repository). Compare the words heard with the line's 'spoken' text, ignoring case and punctuation. A line whose heard words differ from its spoken text goes back to the speak step for that line only; do not accept a line with a missing or changed word. Record each word with its start and end in seconds on the video's timeline (the lines laid end to end with 0.15 seconds between them).

mismatched_lines.description: Lines that still differ from their spoken text after re-speaking; must be empty to continue

steps.title: Make one character, then keep it the same
steps.do: Write the character once in words: input character_description, or invent a simple one (a flat illustrated figure with one identifying mark, a short palette of three colours, and one outfit). Make one base portrait with a local image model from the person's tools, for example a FLUX.2 klein 4B model (weights licensed Apache-2.0, read from the model card; the 9B model has a non-commercial licence and must not be used for a shared video) run through ComfyUI or mflux, whichever the person already has. Keep the character the same in every later picture with this method: pass the base portrait as the reference image to the model's image-edit input together with the same written character description, and keep the seed fixed for the face; when a picture drifts, compare it to the base portrait by looking at both and regenerate it. Then make the mouth shapes: edit only the mouth region of the base portrait into ten shapes from closed to wide open (closed, slightly open, smile, 'oo', 'ee', 'ah', and the intermediate openings), keeping everything else identical. Save the portrait and the ten mouth images and record their paths and the model used with the licence you read.

model.description: The image model, with its licence as read from the model card

checks.says: At least six different mouth openings exist

steps.title: Draw one picture per line with the same character
steps.do: For each line, make its picture with the image model from the make-the-character step: the line's 'picture' idea as the prompt, the base portrait as the reference image, and the written character description. Leave the mouth area as the closed-mouth image; the next step swaps mouths in. Check each picture against the base portrait by looking at both: same face, same mark, same palette, same outfit. Regenerate any that differ. Record which pictures were regenerated and why. Number words are shown in their 'shown' form if a picture prints them.

steps.title: Drive the mouth from the voice's loudness
steps.do: For each audio file, measure loudness at 30 frames per second. Map each frame to one of the mouth images: at or below -42 dB the closed mouth, at or above -16 dB the widest, evenly spaced between; the mouth opens instantly and closes over about half a step per frame (a release of 0.55 per frame), so it never flickers. Add a blink of 0.14 seconds every 2.4 to 4.2 seconds, with the gaps drawn from a fixed random seed so a second render is identical, and a small constant sway. Record, per line, the file that holds the mouth for each frame (frame number to mouth opening). No video model and no outside service is needed: the voice's loudness is the only input.

checks.says: Every line has a mouth track

steps.title: Put it together and render it the same way every time
steps.do: Build the video as one HTML composition for an open-source HTML-to-video renderer from the person's tools: HyperFrames (Apache-2.0, read from its repository) by default. If the person prefers Remotion, read its licence file first: it is free for an individual or a for-profit organisation of up to 3 employees and needs a company licence above that, so say which applies. The composition reads the timed words, the pictures and the mouth tracks as data, with every on-screen change a pure function of time. Captions show each word in light grey and turn it dark at its real start time; each picture appears when its line's first word starts; the voice is at full level and any music bed sits 12 to 14 dB under it, about -14 LUFS overall. Render at the video's size and keep the output path.

renderer.description: The renderer with the licence read from its repository

steps.title: Check the finished video against the lesson
steps.do: Transcribe the finished video's audio with the same local speech-to-text model and compare it to the written lines: zero changed or missing words. Take a frame at the start of each line and look at it: the right picture, the same character, the mouth open when the voice is loud and closed in silence, the caption word lit. Check the length against the plan. List every paid or hosted service used in this run (the answer should be none) and the licence of each model and tool you used, as read from its card or repository. Fix what fails by returning to the step that made it; do not hand over a video with a known miss.

steps.title: Tell the person what was made
steps.do: Call tool:tell-the-person with the path of the finished video and its length, the learner it was pitched at, the voice and character used, the licence of every model and tool, and anything that needs the person (a cloned voice is only made from their own recording; a model whose licence restricts commercial use was not used). Give exact paths, never just 'done'.
